newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Peronists tone down "production ministry" debate.
newsitem.headline: Peronists tone down "production ministry" debate.

text.p: A quarrel in Argentina's Peronist government over proposals for a "Production Ministry" calmed down Thursday when Buenos Aires province Gov. Eduardo Duhalde made concessions to Economy Minister Roque Fernandez.

Duhalde, second-in-command of the Peronist Party and the main contender for the presidential candidacy when Carlos Menem steps down in 1999, said it did not necessarily have to be a new ministry that takes care of production.

"The point is to create a ministry of production or some dependency where small businessmen can be heard," Duhalde told local radio. "I say ministry because that's the strongest way to express it, but it could be some sector working on that."
"It's just a personal opinion. It's ridiculous to think I want to pressure Roque Fernandez," said the governor. "I am sure he knows much more about economy than I do."
Duhalde has been taking issue with the social side-effects of the economic reforms led by Menem since 1989, especially on unemployment, which has more than doubled to over 17 percent.

He laid into Fernandez Wednesday, saying the free-market ideas he espouses "are in retreat" and job creation cannot be left to market forces. "The orthodox theory of adjusting to the market is out of date the world over," he said.
Earlier this week Fernandez shed his usual low profile and held a news conference to argue that Argentina's robust growth showed there was no need for a new ministry.
"It would seem the only opposition that Peronism has are Peronists themselves," said Fernandez, who has tried to avoid infighting since succeeding Domingo Cavallo a year ago.
"If President Carlos Menem was proposing a ministry of production and I disagreed, there would be a conflict, but there isn't because he is not proposing it," he said.

Duhalde and other administration figures considered to be old-fashioned Peronists -- closer to the pro-labor ideals of party founders Juan and Eva Peron -- have been proposing the creation of a production ministry since Cavallo was in power.
Cavallo, now campaigning for an independent seat in Congress, said Thursday that he still believed "it is better for there to be just one team, with one head."

But the ex-minister, who has flirted with supporting Duhalde since he was ousted, included a dig at Fernandez: "If the minister is only taking care of finances and not seeing representatives of the real economy, then another leader is needed."
